item.title: pfoqcompiler: Efficient Compilation of Quantum Control in Recursive First-Order Quantum Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.08503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive quantum control allows for simple and concise descriptions of algorithms. However, a naive circuit compilation sequentializes the different branches of the quantum if-statement and results in an exponential increase in circuit depth. Existing techniques can parallelize these branches, but do so at the cost of an exponential number of ancillary qubits. We present pfoqcompiler, a compiler targeting Qiskit for the first-order quantum programming language FOQ that exploits program structure to merge compatible recursive procedure calls across quantum branches. We introduce weaker syntactically-checkable conditions for well-foundedness, recursive halving, and uniformity, while preserving previously demonstrated complexity characterizations. For weakly well-founded bounded-width programs, the compiler produces polynomial-size circuits; weakly recursively halving programs additionally yield polylogarithmic depth, while weak uniformity removes the asymptotic overhead of branch sequentialization.
item.dc:creator: M\'ario Silva (LMF, QuaCS), Alexandre Guernut (MOCQUA), Marco Lewis (LMF, QuaCS)

item.title: A Complete Calculus for Hamiltonian Quantum Programming
item.description: arXiv:2611.08675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given the forces acting on a quantum particle, a Hamiltonian models its continuous evolution. Quantum computers evolve Hamiltonians to simulate physical systems, to solve optimisation problems, and to estimate eigenvalues, and even the popular circuit abstraction is compiled to Hamiltonians on the hardware. We introduce Hamilton, a process calculus whose parallel operator is the sum of interactions acting simultaneously. Its operational semantics is the Lie-Trotter product formula, which recovers a sum as the limit of ever finer sequential interleavings; compiling a program means halving it to a chosen precision and unrolling the interleaving into a circuit. The semantics is fully abstract, the expressible Hamiltonians are exactly those whose Pauli coefficients have the form $m/2^k$, the precision that successive halving reaches, and the equational theory is complete and decidable. A full implementation compiles Hamilton programs to circuits and decides their equivalence, and Agda proofs sanity-check the core metatheory.
item.dc:creator: Jacques Carette, Chris Heunen, Robin Kaarsgaard, Neil J. Ross, Amr Sabry

item.title: Fibered Separation Logic: Weakest Preconditions, Universal Constructions, and Local Independence
item.description: arXiv:2611.08685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a categorical framework for models of higher-order separation logic including the weakest precondition modality. Weakest preconditions are interpreted by strong monads on a category fibered over a model of Moggi's computational lambda calculus. The fibered categories in question are termed bunched fibrations and shown to be equivalent to BI hyperdoctrines. Well-known heuristic techniques for obtaining weakest preconditions are shown to be expressible in categorical terms and are proved sound. The ``baking in the frame rule'' trick is shown to satisfy a universal property. Constructions are given for extending a program logic with cost credits. Our largest case study is parametrized by a category having local independent product (LIP) structure, a notion due to Simpson that axiomatizes name generation, randomness, and local state. From an LIP category, we construct an allocation monad, a bunched fibration, and a monad lifting. We instantiate our construction to obtain a novel probabilistic separation logic for measure-theoretic probability that both simplifies and clarifies prior work.
item.dc:creator: John M. Li, Ryan Doenges, Pedro H. Azevedo de Amorim

item.title: Nothing Is Shared Until You Synchronise: Reinterpreting Java for Data-Race Freedom
item.description: arXiv:2611.09410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In mainstream shared-memory languages, programmers use synchronisation mechanisms such as locks to isolate shared data accesses across threads to avoid data races. Yet synchronisation enforces only a temporal ordering, while shared memory still communicates updates between threads at every ordinary read and write. To achieve isolation, programmers therefore need to understand the connection between ordering and communication, and to apply synchronisation correctly and consistently, while compilers and hardware optimise assuming they have. When programmers synchronise incorrectly, they lose isolation, and the semantics of their programs change without notice. We propose Sync-as-Share, a memory model built on isolation and communication rather than on the ordering of accesses to shared memory. We start from thread isolation, where each thread reads and writes a private view of memory, and reinterpret programs' existing synchronisation actions to also communicate updates explicitly. As nothing is communicated outside synchronisation actions, data races become impossible by construction. Instead, conflicting updates are detected at synchronisation points. Viewing synchronisation as explicit communication exposes the design decisions of what should be communicated, to whom, and what counts as a conflict. We propose two communication topologies with different trade-offs. We instantiate Sync-as-Share for Java by making the synchronisation actions already defined by its memory model the only points at which threads communicate, so Java programs can adopt Sync-as-Share unmodified. We formalise this instantiation as version-controlled memory, in which synchronisation actions push and pull updates between private views, and mechanise it in Rocq. We show that Java programs that are correctly synchronised under the Java memory model behave identically under shared memory and Sync-as-Share.
item.dc:creator: Luke Cheeseman, Elias Castegren, David Black-Schaffer, Erik \"Osterlund, Tobias Wrigstad

item.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
item.description: arXiv:2611.09822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

item.title: Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09846v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics. We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions.
item.dc:creator: Marco Colombo, Balaji A Jayaram, Sowmyakumari Selvaraj, Sumit Tokkar, Animesh Kumar, Aravinda Prasad Sistla, Ravishankar Shetty, Rigel Gjomemo

item.title: Fuss-free cumulative universes: theory and practice
item.description: arXiv:2607.11329v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Universes are central to dependent type theory, and they are notoriously difficult to handle in a way that is both correct and usable. We propose a new "fuss-free" generalised algebraic presentation for polymorphic cumulative universes that dispenses with the intricate theory of coherent universe coercions in favour of a simpler formulation, which we prove equivalent by means of a normalisation theorem for the former. We study the fuss-free formulation by means of (1) an abstract specification of its bidirectional elaboration algorithm, and (2) a concrete implementation in Haskell. We also describe and implement an extension of the fuss-free universe hierarchy with a judgemental notion of datatype description from which prior notions of cumulative inductive type may be derived.
item.dc:creator: Rapha\"el Sterbac, Jonathan Sterling

item.title: A Physically-Realisable Quantum Programming Language with Quantum-Controlled Quantum Channels
item.description: arXiv:2607.15873v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In contrast to a classical bit, which can only take the value $0$ or $1$, its quantum counterpart---a qubit---can exist in a superposition of $0$ and $1$. This is a superposition of data values, and it is then tempting to superpose programs as well. Indeed, a particular superposition of programs, known as the quantum SWITCH, has attracted considerable attention. A natural way to superpose programs is conditional branching on quantum data, and several studies have pursued this idea. However, there is a well-known semantic difficulty with this approach, and the fundamental question of whether the languages proposed in prior work can be physically realised remains open. This paper proposes a physically realisable quantum programming language with quantum branching over quantum channels. We first analyse the semantic difficulty from an implementation perspective and show that the difficulty is caused by arbitrariness in the implementation. We then design a language that is free from this arbitrariness. As expected from its implementation-oriented design, our language is physically realisable. We argue for this from two directions: first, we give a method for compiling programs into quantum circuits; and second, we show that our programs stay within the physically admissible range, namely, that they neither yield probabilities greater than one nor violate causal inequalities. The absence of such violations is established through the inclusion of our language in QC-QC, a notion of realisability studied in physics.
item.dc:creator: Kengo Hirata, Takeshi Tsukada

item.title: The Program Logic of Abstract Interpretation
item.description: arXiv:2601.20370v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hoare-style program logics and abstract interpretation are two of the principal frameworks for reasoning about programs, and their affinity has long been recognised informally: both derive over-approximate judgements about program behaviour by structural, syntax-directed reasoning. Turning this analogy into a formal correspondence runs into two challenges. First, the disjunction (or join) rule, sound and admissible in Hoare logic, becomes unsound over non-additive abstract semantics. Second, the extrapolation operators that make abstract interpretation effective on unbounded computations, i.e. widening and narrowing, have no analogue in the derivations of existing program logics. We introduce APPL (Abstract Program Property Logic), a Hoare-style program logic that provides a proof-theoretic foundation for abstract interpretation while addressing both challenges. The key technical idea is density: abstract semantics is additive over dense families of logical assertions. This leads to a density-guarded join rule that enables sound disjunctive reasoning over arbitrary abstract domains. We also internalise the application of widening and narrowing through inference rules for iterative commands. As a result, an entire analysis by abstract interpretation can be viewed as a logical derivation in APPL. The logic is sound over any abstract domain and, when the assertion language is expressive enough, it is also relatively complete. Finally, by interpreting nondeterminism through a monoidal operator, APPL provides a single logical framework that uniformly subsumes Hoare logic, incorrectness logic, and Hoare-style logics for hyperproperties, thereby enabling their abstraction. Remarkably, the density-guarded join rule introduced to handle non-additive abstract semantics is also fundamental in guaranteeing completeness for hyperproperties.
item.dc:creator: Paolo Baldan, Roberto Bruni, Francesco Ranzato, Diletta Rigo
